prompt: Code outside `Catalogue` wants to create an `Entry`. How does it name the class?
hint: `main` used this spelling for the third entry.

choices.text: `Entry`, because nested names are visible everywhere in the file's directory
choices.why: The short name works inside `Catalogue` only; outside it, the outer name comes first.

choices.text: `Catalogue.Entry`
choices.why: Right: the outer name, a dot, the inner name.

choices.text: `Catalogue$Entry`
choices.why: That is the name of the class file and of the class at run time; the source writes a dot.

choices.text: `new Catalogue().Entry`, through an object of the outer class
choices.why: A static nested class needs no outer object; that shape belongs to inner classes, with `new` after the dot.

prompt: Compiling `Catalogue.java` wrote two class files: `Catalogue.class` and `___`.
hint: Outer name and inner name, joined by one character.

prompt: `Shelf.Label.text()` reads `capacity`, an instance field of `Shelf`, and the compiler refuses. What is the reason?
hint: Ask which shelf the label would read it from.

choices.text: `capacity` is `private`, and a nested class may not see private members
choices.why: Nested classes do see private members of the outer class; the error message did not mention access.

choices.text: No `Shelf` exists to read it from
choices.why: Right: a static nested object has no outer object, and the message says a static context cannot reach an instance member.

choices.text: Fields of the outer class have to be passed in with `super`
choices.why: `super` reaches a parent class, lesson 20; nesting is not inheritance.

choices.text: `text()` would need to be declared `static` as well
choices.why: A static `text()` has no object either; the field would still have no shelf to come from.

prompt: Which of these may a static nested class `Entry` do inside `Catalogue`? Choose all that apply.
hint: It sits inside the outer class's braces, and it has no outer object.

choices.text: Use a `private static` constant declared in `Catalogue`
choices.why: Yes: nesting puts it inside the line lesson 14 drew, and a static member needs no object.

choices.text: Be created in `main` with no `Catalogue` object
choices.why: Yes: that is how the third entry was made.

choices.text: Read `size`, the instance field of whichever catalogue is current
choices.why: There is no current catalogue for a static nested object; that is `Shelf`'s compile error.

choices.text: Refer to its owner as `Catalogue.this`
choices.why: Only inner classes have an owner to name; a static nested one has none.

prompt: You are writing a `Graph` class and need a small `Edge` type that only `Graph` uses and that holds two node numbers. Following the section's rule of thumb, how do you declare it?
hint: Does an edge need to read the fields of one particular graph?

choices.text: As an inner class, so every edge can reach its graph if it ever needs to
choices.why: That buys a hidden reference in every edge for a need nobody has; the rule says start with `static`.

choices.text: As a `static` nested class of `Graph`
choices.why: Right: it belongs to `Graph`'s implementation and needs no graph object, which is exactly the static nested case.

choices.text: As an anonymous class created inside `Graph`'s constructor
choices.why: An anonymous class makes one object with one job; a graph has many edges of one type.

choices.text: As a separate public class in `Edge.java`
choices.why: That works, and exposes to everyone a type only `Graph` uses; nesting keeps it where it belongs.

prompt: In `main`, how was the first card for Ana created?
hint: `new` was called on something.

choices.text: `new Member.Card(1)`
choices.why: That spelling makes a static nested object; an inner one needs an owner, and the compiler asked for one.

choices.text: `ana.new Card(1)`
choices.why: Right: `new` called on `ana`, which becomes the card's owner.

choices.text: `new Card(ana, 1)`
choices.why: The compiled constructor does take the member first, but the source never writes it that way.

prompt: After `a1.borrow()`, `a2.borrow()` and `r1.borrow()`, what is Ana's `borrowed` count?
hint: Two of the three cards belong to Ana.

prompt: `javap -p 'Member$Card'` listed a field `final Member this$0` that nobody wrote. What is it for?
hint: Where does `name` inside `borrow()` come from?

choices.text: It counts how many cards a member has
choices.why: The count is `borrowed`, an ordinary field of `Member`; `this$0` holds an object, not a number.

choices.text: It is a debugging aid `javap` adds when printing, and is not in the class file
choices.why: `javap` prints what the class file holds; the field is there, and the constructor fills it.

choices.text: The card's owner: `name` compiles into `this$0.name`
choices.why: Right: the compiler turns the owner into a field the JVM understands, filled by the hidden constructor parameter.

choices.text: It points at the first card created, so the others can share its number
choices.why: Each card keeps its own `number`; `this$0` points at a `Member`, not at another card.

prompt: Inside `Card`, what is the difference between `this` and `Member.this`?
hint: `owner()` returns one of them.

choices.text: `this` is the card; `Member.this` is the member it belongs to
choices.why: Right: the long form names the outer object, which `owner()` returns.

choices.text: None: both mean the current object, and the long form is only clearer
choices.why: They are two different objects; `owner() == a2.owner()` would be false if `this` were returned.

choices.text: `this` is the member, and `Member.this` is the class `Member` itself
choices.why: A class is not an object you can reach with `this`; `Member.this` is an object of `Member`.

choices.text: `Member.this` is only allowed inside static methods of `Card`
choices.why: An inner class's static method has no card and no member; the long form is used in instance methods.

prompt: A program keeps a list of event handlers that lives as long as the program. Each handler is an inner class of a large `Report` object, and the reports never seem to leave memory. Why?
hint: Every inner object holds something.

choices.text: Inner classes are loaded once and never unloaded, so their outer objects stay too
choices.why: Classes and objects are different things; what keeps an object alive is a reference to it.

choices.text: Each one's hidden `this$0` points at the object that made it, and stays reachable
choices.why: Right: while the handler is reachable, so is the report it points at; a static nested handler would not hold one.

choices.text: A `Report` cannot be collected until each of its inner classes calls `Report.this.close()`
choices.why: Java has no such rule; lesson 19 shows that reachability alone decides.

choices.text: The JVM copies the report into every handler, multiplying its size
choices.why: Only a reference is stored, not a copy; one report, many arrows to it.

prompt: `new Comparator<String>() { ... }` in `Sorting.java` creates what?
hint: `Comparator` is an interface.

choices.text: An object of the interface `Comparator` itself
choices.why: An interface cannot be instantiated alone; the braces supply a class.

choices.text: A new named class called `Comparator` that replaces the JDK's
choices.why: It has no name in the source, and the compiler called it `Sorting$1`.

choices.text: One object of a class with no name, supplying the missing `compare`
choices.why: Right: declared and instantiated in one expression, with `compare` supplied in the braces.

prompt: Why did the plain `Arrays.sort(titles)` put `effective Java` last?
hint: Compare the first letters' codes.

choices.text: Strings are sorted by length, and it is the shortest
choices.why: `Head First Java` is shorter than `Modern Java in Action` and came first, so length was not the order.

choices.text: Capitals sort before small letters, and it starts with `e`
choices.why: Right: the comparator that ignores case put it first.

choices.text: `sort` keeps the array's original order for strings it cannot compare
choices.why: Every pair of strings can be compared; the order is the natural one, by code.

choices.text: Arrays are sorted from the end, and it was the second element
choices.why: It was second in the source array; sorting does not start from the end.

prompt: Match each class the lesson compiled to the name of its class file.
hint: `ls` printed each one.

prompt: Adding `days = 21;` made `Overdue.java` fail to compile. Which line did the error point at?
hint: Read the caret.

choices.text: The new assignment `days = 21;`
choices.why: The assignment is legal on its own; the error is where the class reads the variable.

choices.text: The use of `days` inside `Notice.text`
choices.why: Right: line 7, where the local class reads a variable that is no longer effectively final.

choices.text: The declaration `int days = 14;`, which should have said `final`
choices.why: Writing `final` would make the assignment illegal instead; the message pointed at the read.

prompt: Why does Java insist that a captured local variable be effectively final, rather than letting the class see later changes?
hint: What does the object actually hold?

choices.text: Because changing a local variable from two places at once is a race between threads
choices.why: The rule holds in single-threaded code too, as `Overdue` showed.

choices.text: Because the class runs before the method's later statements
choices.why: The class runs when its method is called, which can be any time.

choices.text: The object holds a copy taken at creation, which would go stale
choices.why: Right: the compiler copies the value into a field; Java refuses rather than let the two disagree.

choices.text: Because local variables are deleted when the class is compiled
choices.why: Local variables live in the method's frame while it runs; compilation deletes nothing.

prompt: Since Java 8, what usually replaces an anonymous class that implements a one-method interface such as `Comparator`?
hint: `java-functional` starts there.

choices.text: A static nested class
choices.why: That needs a name and a declaration; it is longer, not shorter.

choices.text: A lambda expression
choices.why: Right: `(a, b) -> a.compareToIgnoreCase(b)` is the same comparator in one line.

choices.text: A local class
choices.why: A local class is still a full class declaration, used by one method.

prompt: Order the four kinds from the one tied to nothing to the one that exists only inside a single expression.
hint: The table at the end of section 04.

prompt: A `Parser` reads a file and needs a small `Token` type that records the token's text and its position in the file. No token needs to read the parser's fields. Which declaration fits, and what does the wrong choice cost?
hint: Count what each token would carry as an inner class.

choices.text: An inner class; static nested would make every token share one text
choices.why: Fields of a nested object are per object either way; `static` on the class does not make its fields static.

choices.text: A static nested class; as an inner class each of thousands of tokens would also hold the parser
choices.why: Right: a hidden `this$0` per token, for a need no token has, and the parser kept alive by any token still referenced.

choices.text: An anonymous class, created once per token inside the read loop
choices.why: An anonymous class is one class; using it as a data type gives a type nobody can name in a variable.

choices.text: Either: static and inner differ only in how the class is written
choices.why: They differ in a field every object carries, as `javap` showed.

prompt: Which of these compiles in `Member.main` as written in the lesson?
hint: `main` is static, so it has no `this`.

choices.text: `Member.Card c = new Card(9);`
choices.why: That was the edited line, and the compiler said `this` cannot be referenced from a static context.

choices.text: `Member.Card c = Member.this.new Card(9);`
choices.why: `Member.this` is the outer object of an inner one; in a static method there is none.

choices.text: `Member.Card c = rui.new Card(9);`
choices.why: Right: `rui` is an existing member, and it becomes the card's owner.

choices.text: `Member.Card c = new Member.Card(9);`
choices.why: The outer name does not supply an outer object; an inner class still needs one.

prompt: A local variable that is never changed after it is first set, whether or not it says `final`, is called effectively ___.
hint: Two words in English, and the course keeps them in English.
